Distribution
dis-tri-bu'shun
n. (the dealing out of goods to those in need; of the Jerusalem church's care of its poor, and of the Corinthian collection Paul gathered for famine relief)
From Latin distribuere, to deal out, from dis- and tribuere, to assign. The Greek at Acts 4:35 is diadidomi, to give out among; at 2 Corinthians 9:13 the word is koinonia, fellowship — the sharing itself.

Biblical Definition

Luke describes the practice of the Jerusalem church in terms that have been misread in every century since. Possessors of lands or houses sold them and brought the prices, “And laid them down at the apostles' feet: and distribution was made unto every man according as he had need” (Acts 4:35), with the result stated first: “Neither was there any among them that lacked” (Acts 4:34). Four features govern the account. The selling was voluntary — Peter tells Ananias that the land was his own and the price was in his own power. It was occasional, not a permanent surrender of all property, since believers still met in houses. It was administered by the apostles and soon delegated to deacons. And the measure was need. Paul's word for the same thing among the Gentile churches is koinonia: “for your liberal distribution unto them, and unto all men” (2 Corinthians 9:13), and he notes that the recipients glorify God for it. The command to the rich is put in the same register: “that they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate” (1 Timothy 6:18).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines distribution as the act of dividing among a number, dealing out in parts or portions — and in a scriptural sense, the giving of alms.

expand to see more

DISTRIBUTION, n. The act of dividing among a number; a dealing in parts or portions.

2. The act of giving in charity; the bestowment of alms.

3. Dispensation; administration to numbers.

DISTRIBUTE, v.t. To divide among two or more; to deal out; to give or bestow in parts or portions.

COMMUNICATE, v.i. To share with others; to impart a portion of what one has.

Key Scripture

Acts 4:34 — "Neither was there any among them that lacked: for as many as were possessors of lands or houses sold them, and brought the prices of the things that were sold,"

Acts 4:35 — "And laid them down at the apostles' feet: and distribution was made unto every man according as he had need."

2 Corinthians 9:13 — "Whiles by the experiment of this ministration they glorify God for your professed subjection unto the gospel of Christ, and for your liberal distribution unto them, and unto all men;"

1 Timothy 6:18 — "That they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate;"

Modern Corruption

Acts 4 is claimed as a mandate for compulsory collectivism on one side and explained away entirely on the other; the text supports neither.

expand to see more

The passage has been enlisted for two centuries as scriptural warrant for common ownership imposed by authority, and the enlistment fails on Peter's own words to Ananias: Whiles it remained, was it not thine own? and after it was sold, was it not in thine own power? The sin was the lie, not the withholding, and the question presupposes a right of private property that the apostle does not dispute. Nor did the practice abolish households; the church continued to meet from house to house, and Mary the mother of John Mark still had a home in Jerusalem in chapter twelve. What is described is voluntary, occasional, need-measured liquidation by believers under extraordinary pressure, administered by the church for its own poor.

The opposite error is to explain the chapter away so thoroughly that nothing is required of anyone. Luke states the outcome as a commendation: neither was there any among them that lacked, and he says it twice in two chapters. Paul organised a transcontinental collection over years, carried it with a delegation so that no man could suspect the handling, and described its aim as an equality — that the abundance of one might supply the want of another. A congregation in which members lack necessities while others have abundance has not preserved a doctrine of property; it has failed a plain apostolic standard.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek diadidomi, to distribute — Acts 4:35; koinonia, fellowship, sharing — 2 Corinthians 9:13; eumetadotos, ready to distribute — 1 Timothy 6:18.

expand to see more

Greek diadidomi — to give out among, distribute; Acts 4:35.

Greek koinonia — fellowship, communion, and so a contribution shared; 2 Corinthians 9:13.

Greek eumetadotos — ready to impart; 1 Timothy 6:18, its only New Testament occurrence.

Greek koinonikos — willing to communicate, sociable in giving; the companion word in the same verse.

Greek chreia — need; Acts 4:35, the measure of the distribution.

Usage

"“Distribution was made unto every man according as he had need” — need was the measure."

"“Neither was there any among them that lacked” — the outcome Luke commends."

"“Ready to distribute, willing to communicate” — the charge to the rich."
